screens.title: Global Reach and DNS: CloudFront & Route 53
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll build a mental model of two complementary services: Amazon CloudFront, which gets your content physically closer to users, and Amazon Route 53, which directs users to the right endpoint. You will understand why a CDN matters for latency, how edge locations cache and serve content, and the role of origins and origin access control in protecting S3-hosted assets. You’ll also learn how Route 53 acts as the domain name system for your application: hosted zones contain records, Alias records let you point a zone apex to AWS resources, and routing policies control how DNS answers users. A concrete outcome of this chapter is the ability to host a static site in S3, restrict bucket access to CloudFront, create a CloudFront distribution with a custom certificate, and map a friendly domain name with a Route 53 hosted zone and an Alias A record. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls — for example, forgetting to use Origin Access Control or failing to update your registrar’s name servers — and practical checks like validating DNS propagation and denying raw S3 requests. By the end you’ll see how CDN and DNS together shape global performance and reliability.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to practical competencies you will acquire. First, you will explain the benefits of using Amazon CloudFront as a global CDN: how caching at edge locations reduces latency and offloads origin servers. I will show you a concrete example of a static file request served from the nearest edge, and why that matters for real users. Second, you will configure a CloudFront distribution with an S3 origin and set up Origin Access Control so the bucket is only readable through CloudFront; we'll discuss the common misconfiguration that either exposes the bucket or blocks CloudFront. Third, you'll describe Route 53 as a highly available DNS service, understand hosted zones and record sets, and why delegating name servers at your registrar is essential. Finally, you will create and manage Route 53 hosted zones and implement routing policies such as simple, weighted, and latency-based routing for different operational goals. Each objective pairs a technical skill with an operational rationale and a verification milestone so you can measure competency.

screens.title: What is Amazon CloudFront?
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that places cached copies of your content at edge locations around the world. The essential claim is simple: by moving content closer to users, the network reduces round-trip time and speeds page loads. A concrete example: when an image request arrives from Paris, CloudFront routes the request to the nearest point of presence; if the image is cached there, it returns immediately instead of fetching it from an S3 bucket in another region. This reduces latency and the load on your origin. CloudFront supports static assets, dynamic content, APIs, and streaming, and it integrates with origins such as S3, an Application Load Balancer, or an HTTP server. A common misconception is that CDNs only help large media files; in reality, small assets like C S S and JavaScript also benefit because many users request them repeatedly. Another pitfall is assuming CloudFront automatically caches everything forever; caching respects origin headers and your cache behaviors, so you must intentionally set TTLs. Key takeaway: CloudFront is about proximity and caching policy — know what to cache, for how long, and which requests should bypass cache. To check understanding, name one asset on your site that should be cached aggressively and one that should not.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CloudFront caches content at edge locations to deliver data with low latency and reduce load on origins.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › What is CloudFront?
Core Concept

CloudFront explained

CloudFront places cached content at edge locations to serve users with lower latency and to offload origin servers.

How it works
  • Client request routes to the nearest edge location (PoP).
  • If content is cached, it returns immediately; otherwise CloudFront fetches from the origin and caches it.
  • Cache behavior and TTLs control how objects are stored and refreshed.
Concrete example

A static logo served from CloudFront reaches European users from a nearby edge instead of the origin region, improving perceived load time.

Key Takeaway

Use CloudFront for global distribution of assets; set explicit caching policies for the right balance between freshness and performance.

Illustration
Edge Location (PoP)
Nearest cache that serves repeated requests
Remember: caching small and repeated assets yields substantial latency improvement for many users.
Common misconception
It’s not enough to enable CloudFront — you must also set cache behaviors and TTLs. Otherwise content may be stale or not cached effectively.

screens.title: Edge Locations and Caching Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the request flow is essential to control latency and consistency. When a client asks for an object, DNS directs it to a CloudFront domain; CloudFront then routes that request to the nearest edge location. If the requested object is cached at the edge, CloudFront returns it immediately. If not, the edge forwards the request to the origin, retrieves the object, caches it according to your cache behavior, and returns it to the client. Cache behaviors let you define which paths are cached, which HTTP methods are allowed, and whether to forward query strings or cookies. For example, static images benefit from long TTLs, while A P I responses typically bypass caching or use short TTLs. A common mistake is leaving cache-control headers unset at the origin; CloudFront will follow those headers, so missing directives can mean no caching or unintended staleness. A practical example: set Cache-Control: max-age=86400 for static assets and use a shorter TTL for assets that change frequently. Finally, remember that invalidation is a tool for immediate updates but can incur cost and should be used sparingly. As a reflective prompt, consider which assets on your site need immediate invalidation versus versioned filenames.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Requests hit the nearest edge; cache behaviors and origin headers determine whether content is served from cache or fetched from the origin.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Edge Locations & Caching
Process Flow

Request lifecycle

1) DNS resolves the CloudFront domain and the client reaches the nearest edge PoP.
2) Edge checks local cache. If a hit occurs, the object is served immediately with low latency.
3) On a cache miss, the edge requests the object from the origin, caches it according to cache behavior and origin headers, and returns it to the client.
4) Cache behaviors control TTL, allowed methods, and whether to forward query strings, cookies, or headers.
Example

Set Cache-Control: max-age=86400 for images to keep them in edge caches for a day, and use short TTLs or no-cache for API endpoints.

Cache Behavior Cards
Static assets
Long TTLs, GET/HEAD only, forward minimal headers.
Dynamic content / APIs
Short TTLs or no-cache, allow additional methods, forward query strings and authorization headers when needed.
Invalidation
Use to remove cached objects immediately, but prefer versioned filenames when possible to avoid costs.
Key Takeaway

Design cache behaviors and origin headers deliberately: they decide what is fast, what is fresh, and what stays on your origin.

screens.title: Origins and Origin Access Control (OAC)
screens.narratorSegment: Origins are the authoritative source of your content. They can be S3 buckets for static assets, an Application Load Balancer for dynamic services, or any HTTP server. When you use an S3 bucket as an origin, a best practice is to prevent direct public access and allow CloudFront to retrieve objects on your behalf. Origin Access Control, or OAC, is the recommended way to do this: you create an OAC identity in CloudFront, which is the identity CloudFront uses when it fetches from S3. After creating the OAC, CloudFront produces a bucket policy snippet you add to your S3 bucket permissions so only that OAC can GetObject. A common misstep is enabling static website hosting on S3 and leaving the bucket public; that bypasses the CDN and exposes raw URLs. Another error is misapplying the bucket policy so CloudFront is blocked. To verify OAC, attempt to fetch an object directly from the S3 URL; it should be denied, while requests to your CloudFront domain should succeed. Practically, OAC protects your origin while delivering via CloudFront, combining security and caching benefits. Consider whether any backend needs direct access; if not, lock down the bucket tightly.

keyIdea.title: Origin security
keyIdea.text: Use Origin Access Control so the S3 bucket accepts requests only from CloudFront and denies direct public access.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Origins & OAC
Architecture

Origin types and OAC

Origins provide the original content. For S3 origins, use Origin Access Control to grant CloudFront read permissions and block public access.

Common origins
  • S3 bucket for static assets.
  • Application Load Balancer for dynamic backends.
  • Custom HTTP servers for specialized content.
OAC workflow
  1. Create OAC in CloudFront and attach it to the origin.
  2. Copy the bucket policy CloudFront provides into the S3 bucket policy.
  3. Enable "Block all public access" on the bucket so only CloudFront can read objects.
Mistake to avoid

Do not enable S3 static website hosting for a CloudFront origin if you intend to deny direct access; it can expose raw URLs and bypass CloudFront protections.

Quick test

After applying OAC and the bucket policy, try fetching the object directly via the S3 URL — the request should be denied. Then request the same object via the CloudFront domain — it should succeed and be cached at the edge.

Key Takeaway

Origin Access Control secures S3 origins while preserving CloudFront caching benefits; always test direct and CDN requests after setup.

screens.title: Preparing Static Content and S3 Bucket
screens.narratorSegment: Before creating a distribution, prepare the origin. For a static website example the chapter provides, create an S3 bucket named to match your desired host, such as www. yourdomain. com, and upload an index. html and optionally an error. html. Crucially, do not enable S3 static website hosting; it lets users bypass CloudFront. Instead, keep the bucket private and rely on Origin Access Control. A concrete content example is a simple index. html with a single heading, which you can upload to verify path and default root object. Once uploaded, set the bucket to block public access, and later you will paste the bucket policy CloudFront provides to allow only the OAC identity to read objects. This practice enforces that users only obtain files through CloudFront, which ensures TLS termination, caching, and any custom behaviors you configure. A common trap is giving overly broad bucket policies; always scope permissions to the CloudFront OAC identity. Preparing Static Content and S3 Bucket means upload your static files to a private s3 bucket, do not enable static website hosting, and prepare to apply a cloudfront-generated bucket policy for oac.. In practical terms, upload index.html and set bucket properties for cloudfront. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Setup
keyIdea.text: Upload your static files to a private S3 bucket, do not enable static website hosting, and prepare to apply a CloudFront-generated bucket policy for OAC.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Prepare S3 Content
Definition

Static assets and bucket configuration

Upload your static files, keep the bucket private, and plan to use Origin Access Control to permit only CloudFront to read objects.

Why not enable static website hosting?

Static website hosting exposes public URLs that bypass CloudFront; to enforce CDN behavior and TLS, leave hosting off and use OAC.

Example index.html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Hello from CloudFront</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello from CloudFront!</h1>
  </body>
</html>
Upload this index.html as the default root object and confirm it renders via CloudFront once the distribution is deployed.
Pro tip

Use versioned filenames for assets to avoid frequent invalidations when updating static files.

screens.title: Cache-Control and TTLs: Freshness vs Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Designing cache lifetimes is a trade-off between freshness and performance. Long TTLs keep objects at the edge longer and reduce origin traffic; they are ideal for static images and versioned assets. Short TTLs or no-cache are better for frequently changing content or personalized responses. Invalidation lets you remove objects from edge caches immediately, but invalidations can increase origin load and may incur cost or delay. A recommended pattern is to use long TTLs for public static content and rely on asset versioning — change the file name when content updates — so you avoid invalidations. For dynamic endpoints, use short TTLs and configure CloudFront to forward relevant headers or query strings so caching is correct per user or session. A misconception is to set a universal TTL for all assets; instead, classify assets by update cadence. As an exercise, think of three assets in your application and assign one of: long TTL with versioning, short TTL, or no caching. That classification will guide cache behaviors and origin header settings. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Cache-Control Strategies

Freshness vs Performance

Choose TTLs and invalidation strategies based on asset update frequency and user impact.

Long TTL
Use for static, versioned assets. Reduces origin load and speeds delivery.
Short TTL
Use for content that changes frequently or is user-specific.
Invalidation
Immediate removal of cached objects; use sparingly and prefer versioning.
Example classifications
  • Logo image: long TTL + versioned filename.
  • Main page HTML: short TTL or cache-control sensitive to updates.
  • User dashboard API: no-cache or very short TTL, forward authorization headers.
Key Takeaway

Classify assets by update frequency and use versioning to minimize invalidations while maximizing performance.

screens.title: Common CloudFront Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When CloudFront doesn't behave as expected, the root cause often lies in caching rules, origin permissions, or certificate and domain settings. A frequent issue is missing or incorrect Origin Access Control configuration: either the bucket remains public or CloudFront cannot access objects. To troubleshoot, check bucket policies and the S3 console's public access settings; confirm that the policy grants GetObject permission only to the CloudFront OAC identity. Another common problem is improper cache-control headers causing either stale content or no caching; inspect responses from the origin for correct Cache-Control directives. Custom domain and TLS issues usually stem from using the wrong certificate region — CloudFront requires the certificate in the correct place — and failing to add the distribution domain to Alternate Domain Names. DNS problems typically involve failing to update your registrar's name servers after creating a hosted zone. Practical checks: fetch an object from the raw S3 URL, fetch the same object via the CloudFront domain, and perform a DNS lookup to ensure your Alias record resolves to the distribution. As a guiding question, when you see stale content, what two things would you check first? Cache headers and whether an invalidation or versioning strategy was applied.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot
keyIdea.text: Check OAC permissions, cache-control headers, certificate placement, and registrar name-server delegation when diagnosing issues.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › CloudFront Mistakes

Common mistakes

OAC misconfigured: Either bucket left public or CloudFront blocked.
Cache headers missing: Cache-Control absent or incorrect causes stale data or no caching.
Registrar not updated: Hosted zone NS records not set at registrar prevents domain resolution.
Certificate region issue: Custom SSL misplacement prevents secure custom domain use with CloudFront.
Troubleshooting checklist
  1. Attempt a direct S3 object fetch; expect denial when OAC is correct.
  2. Fetch the same object through CloudFront; verify it returns and is cached.
  3. Check response headers for Cache-Control and age values to understand caching behavior.
  4. Verify Route 53 Alias record and name-server delegation at your registrar.
Pro tip

When updating many files, prefer versioned filenames to avoid bulk invalidations and reduce risk of origin overload.

screens.title: Amazon Route 53 Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Route 53 is AWS's scalable DNS service. At its core, DNS translates human-friendly domain names into machine-readable addresses. A hosted zone in Route 53 is a container for the resource records that define how traffic for a domain and its subdomains should be routed. When you create a hosted zone, Route 53 assigns name servers — typically four NS records — that you must copy to your domain registrar to delegate authority. Without that delegation your hosted zone won't control queries for the domain. Inside a hosted zone you create record sets: A and AAAA records map names to IPv4 or IPv6 addresses; CNAME maps one name to another but cannot be used at the zone apex; Alias records are an AWS-specific option that act like a CNAME but can be placed at the zone apex and point to AWS resources such as CloudFront or an ELB. A practical example: create a hosted zone for yourdomain. com, copy NS records to the registrar, and add an Alias A record for www pointing to your CloudFront distribution. A common misconception is that creating records in Route 53 alone is enough — you must also update your registrar to use the Route 53 name servers. Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Route 53 Fundamentals

Hosted zones and Name Servers

A hosted zone stores record sets for a domain. To make Route 53 authoritative, copy the assigned NS records to your registrar.

Hosted zone: container for records that route traffic for a domain and subdomains.
NS records: four name servers you copy to your registrar to delegate DNS authority.
Record sets: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, and Alias records define routing behavior.
Key Takeaway

Creating records in Route 53 is necessary but not sufficient; remember to update your registrar with Route 53's NS records to delegate your domain.

Practical example
Create a public hosted zone for yourdomain.com, copy the four NS records, and paste them into your domain registrar's name-server settings. Then create an Alias A record for www that points to your CloudFront distribution.
Note
Use Alias records instead of CNAME at the zone apex; Alias behaves like a CNAME for AWS resources but can be used at the root domain.

screens.title: Route 53 Record Types and Alias Records
screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 supports common DNS record types and an AWS-specific Alias record. Use A and AAAA records to map names to IPv4 or IPv6 addresses when you have concrete IP endpoints. Use CNAME to map a subdomain to another domain name, but remember CNAMEs cannot be used at the zone apex, so you cannot make example. com a CNAME to another host. Alias records are an AWS extension that act like a CNAME but can be used at the zone apex and can point to CloudFront distributions, ELBs, and other AWS resources. Alias records are free and resolve to the IP addresses of the target resource, making them ideal for routing the root domain to a CloudFront distribution. Another common use case is MX records for mail servers and NS records for delegation. A practical example: to map www. yourdomain. com to a CloudFront distribution, create an Alias A record for www pointing to the distribution. The misconception to avoid is treating an Alias as identical to a CNAME; while they behave similarly for name resolution, Alias records are specially integrated with AWS targets and support apex routing.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Record Types

A, CNAME, and Alias

Choose the record type that fits your target and whether apex routing is required.

A / AAAA
Map a name to IPv4 or IPv6 addresses directly.
CNAME
Alias a subdomain to another domain name; cannot be used at the zone apex.
Alias (AWS)
Acts like a CNAME but can be used at the zone apex and points directly to AWS resources such as CloudFront.
Practical example
To use yourdomain.com as the primary site and point it at a CloudFront distribution, create an Alias A record at the zone apex that routes to the distribution. CNAME would not be valid at the apex.
Key Takeaway

Use Alias records for apex routing to AWS endpoints; prefer Alias for CloudFront integrations.

screens.title: Route 53 Routing Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 offers several routing policies to meet operational goals. Simple routing sends all traffic to one resource, which is easy but provides no distribution. Weighted routing lets you split traffic based on weights — for example, 80% to a primary environment and 20% to a canary — useful for A/B testing or gradual rollouts. Latency-based routing sends users to the region offering the lowest latency, which is appropriate for multi-region deployments where performance is the priority. Geolocation routing sends requests based on the user's geographic location, useful for legal or content localization needs. Failover routing works with Route 53 health checks to send traffic to a secondary resource when the primary is unhealthy. Multivalue answer routing returns multiple healthy records to clients, allowing client-side retry across addresses. A typical production pattern is to use latency-based routing across multiple regions and failover routing with health checks for resilience. When designing routing, think about the user experience you want: predictable distribution, fastest path, regional control, or automated failover. For validation, test from multiple geographic vantage points and simulate endpoint failure to ensure failover behaves correctly.

keyIdea.title: Routing
keyIdea.text: Choose routing policies according to goals: weighted for experiments, latency for performance, geolocation for compliance, and failover for resilience.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Routing Policies

Choose a routing policy

Simple: single resource, straightforward.
Weighted: split traffic by weight for experiments or staged rollouts.
Latency-based: route to the region with the lowest network latency.
Geolocation: route based on the user's geographic location.
Failover: primary/secondary routing using health checks for automatic failover.
Example scenarios
  • Multi-region app: latency-based routing to send users to the fastest region.
  • Canary release: weighted routing with 5–10% traffic to the new version.
  • Critical service: failover routing with Route 53 health checks to enable automatic failover to a standby endpoint.
Key Takeaway

Align routing policy with your operational objective: performance, testing, geographic control, or resilience, and validate with tests from multiple locations.

screens.title: Activity Walkthrough: S3 → CloudFront → Route 53
screens.narratorSegment: This activity ties together the chapter: host a static website in S3, distribute it with CloudFront, and map a custom domain with Route 53. Step one: create an S3 bucket named to match your host, upload index. html and error. html, and keep public access blocked. Step two: in CloudFront create a distribution with that S3 bucket as the origin. Choose Origin Access Control and create a new OAC identity. After creating the OAC, copy the bucket policy CloudFront generates into your S3 bucket policy so only CloudFront can read objects. Step three: in Route 53 create a public hosted zone for yourdomain. com, copy the four NS records to your registrar and wait for delegation. This step-by-step practice demonstrates the integration points and where to perform verification checks. After completing it, reflect on which verification step gave you confidence the setup was secure and performant.

keyIdea.title: Lab summary
keyIdea.text: Follow the ordered steps: upload to S3, create CloudFront with OAC, apply bucket policy, create hosted zone and Alias record, then verify end-to-end.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Activity Walkthrough

Deploy a static site: high-level steps

1. Upload to S3
Create bucket named www.yourdomain.com, upload index.html, keep bucket private, do not enable static website hosting.
2. Create CloudFront
Select S3 origin, create OAC, set viewer protocol to redirect to HTTPS, set default root object to index.html.
3. Apply bucket policy
Copy CloudFront’s suggested policy into your S3 bucket to allow only the OAC to get objects.
4. Route 53 hosted zone
Create hosted zone, copy NS records to your registrar, and wait for delegation.
5. Alias record
Create an Alias A record for www.yourdomain.com pointing to the CloudFront distribution.
6. Test & verify
Open https://www.yourdomain.com and confirm the content. Try a direct S3 object URL — it should be denied.
Key Takeaway

Complete each step and verify both CDN delivery and origin protection to ensure a secure, global static site deployment.

screens.title: Key Concepts — CloudFront & Route 53

Origins can be S3, ALB, or custom HTTP servers; for S3 origins, use Origin Access Control to prevent direct public access and allow only CloudFront to read objects. Route 53 is a DNS service: create hosted zones and copy the NS records to your registrar to delegate DNS. Use Alias records to point the zone apex to AWS targets like CloudFront. Before you finish, remember to verify configurations: test a direct S3 fetch, test the CloudFront URL, and perform DNS lookups to confirm delegation. These checks help avoid downtime and exposure of raw assets.

Global CDN that caches content at edge locations to reduce latency and origin load.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Finally, keep three practical reminders close by. First, always lock down S3 buckets intended as CloudFront origins and grant access only to the OAC identity; this prevents raw S3 URL access. Use Origin Access Control and a strict bucket policy so only CloudFront reads S3 objects.

In this lesson we’ll build a mental model of two complementary services: Amazon CloudFront, which gets your content physically closer to users, and Amazon Route 53, which directs users to the right endpoint. You will understand why a CDN matters for latency, how edge locations cache and serve content, and the role of origins and origin access control in protecting S3-hosted assets. You’ll also learn how Route 53 acts as the domain name system for your application: hosted zones contain records, Alias records let you point a zone apex to AWS resources, and routing policies control how DNS answers users. A concrete outcome of this chapter is the ability to host a static site in S3, restrict bucket access to CloudFront, create a CloudFront distribution with a custom certificate, and map a friendly domain name with a Route 53 hosted zone and an Alias A record. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls — for example, forgetting to use Origin Access Control or failing to update your registrar’s name servers — and practical checks like validating DNS propagation and denying raw S3 requests. By the end you’ll see how CDN and DNS together shape global performance and reliability.

These learning objectives map to practical competencies you will acquire. First, you will explain the benefits of using Amazon CloudFront as a global CDN: how caching at edge locations reduces latency and offloads origin servers. I will show you a concrete example of a static file request served from the nearest edge, and why that matters for real users. Second, you will configure a CloudFront distribution with an S3 origin and set up Origin Access Control so the bucket is only readable through CloudFront; we'll discuss the common misconfiguration that either exposes the bucket or blocks CloudFront. Third, you'll describe Route 53 as a highly available DNS service, understand hosted zones and record sets, and why delegating name servers at your registrar is essential. Finally, you will create and manage Route 53 hosted zones and implement routing policies such as simple, weighted, and latency-based routing for different operational goals. Each objective pairs a technical skill with an operational rationale and a verification milestone so you can measure competency.

This second objectives slide emphasizes verification and practical checks. You will learn to validate CloudFront deployment and check that the S3 bucket denies direct access while CloudFront can fetch objects. I will outline how to confirm DNS changes: create a hosted zone in Route 53, copy its NS records to your registrar, and verify that the domain resolves to the CloudFront distribution with an Alias A record. You will also practice using routing policies: weighted routing for gradual rollouts, and latency-based routing to send users to the fastest region. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or verification step such as running a DNS lookup to confirm NS delegation or attempting to fetch the raw S3 URL to confirm OAC. We emphasize simple, repeatable checks because misconfiguration leads to downtime or exposed content. After these objectives you will be ready to complete the hands-on activity of deploying a static site behind CloudFront and mapping it to a friendly domain name.

Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that places cached copies of your content at edge locations around the world. The essential claim is simple: by moving content closer to users, the network reduces round-trip time and speeds page loads. A concrete example: when an image request arrives from Paris, CloudFront routes the request to the nearest point of presence; if the image is cached there, it returns immediately instead of fetching it from an S3 bucket in another region. This reduces latency and the load on your origin. CloudFront supports static assets, dynamic content, APIs, and streaming, and it integrates with origins such as S3, an Application Load Balancer, or an HTTP server. A common misconception is that CDNs only help large media files; in reality, small assets like C S S and JavaScript also benefit because many users request them repeatedly. Another pitfall is assuming CloudFront automatically caches everything forever; caching respects origin headers and your cache behaviors, so you must intentionally set TTLs. Key takeaway: CloudFront is about proximity and caching policy — know what to cache, for how long, and which requests should bypass cache. To check understanding, name one asset on your site that should be cached aggressively and one that should not.

Understanding the request flow is essential to control latency and consistency. When a client asks for an object, DNS directs it to a CloudFront domain; CloudFront then routes that request to the nearest edge location. If the requested object is cached at the edge, CloudFront returns it immediately. If not, the edge forwards the request to the origin, retrieves the object, caches it according to your cache behavior, and returns it to the client. Cache behaviors let you define which paths are cached, which HTTP methods are allowed, and whether to forward query strings or cookies. For example, static images benefit from long TTLs, while A P I responses typically bypass caching or use short TTLs. A common mistake is leaving cache-control headers unset at the origin; CloudFront will follow those headers, so missing directives can mean no caching or unintended staleness. A practical example: set Cache-Control: max-age=86400 for static assets and use a shorter TTL for assets that change frequently. Finally, remember that invalidation is a tool for immediate updates but can incur cost and should be used sparingly. As a reflective prompt, consider which assets on your site need immediate invalidation versus versioned filenames.

Origins are the authoritative source of your content. They can be S3 buckets for static assets, an Application Load Balancer for dynamic services, or any HTTP server. When you use an S3 bucket as an origin, a best practice is to prevent direct public access and allow CloudFront to retrieve objects on your behalf. After creating the OAC, CloudFront produces a bucket policy snippet you add to your S3 bucket permissions so only that OAC can GetObject. A common misstep is enabling static website hosting on S3 and leaving the bucket public; that bypasses the CDN and exposes raw URLs. Another error is misapplying the bucket policy so CloudFront is blocked. To verify OAC, attempt to fetch an object directly from the S3 URL; it should be denied, while requests to your CloudFront domain should succeed. Practically, OAC protects your origin while delivering via CloudFront, combining security and caching benefits. Before creating a distribution, prepare the origin. These rules reduce user-facing latency, prevent accidental exposure, and make DNS-based routing predictable. As you move from lab to production, add health checks and consider routing policies such as latency-based routing for multi-region deployments and failover with health checks for resilience. Ask yourself on each deployment: have I tested direct origin denial, CDN delivery, and DNS resolution?
